title: The First Letter to the Corinthians
subtitle: Pros Korinthious A, “First to the Corinthians”
description: Paul’s letter to a gifted, quarrelsome church in one of the busiest cities of the Roman world, and the fullest picture the New Testament gives of a congregation’s life from the inside. Rival parties rallying round favourite teachers, answered by “Christ crucified”, the foolishness of God that is wiser than human wisdom; the body as a temple of the Holy Spirit; marriage and singleness; food offered to idols, and the freedom that gives way for a brother or sister for whom Christ died; the Lord’s Supper; one body with many parts; the chapter on love; and the great chapter on the resurrection of the dead: “Death, where is your victory?” In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is 1 Corinthians?
qa.answer: The seventh book of the New Testament, a letter from the apostle Paul to the church he had founded in Corinth, in Greece. It answers a report of divisions in the church and a letter of questions the Corinthians had sent him, on matters ranging from lawsuits and marriage to food offered to idols, the Lord’s Supper and spiritual gifts. It contains the chapter on love (13), the earliest written account of the Lord’s Supper (11:23–26) and the fullest teaching on the resurrection in the New Testament (15).

qa.question: Who wrote 1 Corinthians, and when?
qa.answer: The apostle Paul, who names himself in the first verse, together with a fellow believer called Sosthenes. Almost all scholars accept that Paul wrote it. He sent it from Ephesus (16:8), probably around AD 53–55, a few years after he had spent a year and a half founding the church in Corinth (Acts 18). It was not his first letter to them: he mentions an earlier one (5:9) that has not survived.

qa.question: Why did Paul write 1 Corinthians?
qa.answer: Members of Chloe’s household had told him that the church was splitting into factions, each claiming a favourite leader: Paul, Apollos, Cephas or Christ (1:11–12). He had also heard of sexual immorality and lawsuits among them, and the church had written to him with questions about marriage, food offered to idols, spiritual gifts and other matters, often introduced in the letter with “Now about”. Some were also denying the resurrection of the dead. Paul answers each of these, bringing them all back to the cross and resurrection of Christ.

qa.question: What does 1 Corinthians 13 say about love?
qa.answer: That without love, even the greatest gifts, knowledge, faith and sacrifice count for nothing, and that love is patient and kind, does not envy or show off, does not keep a tally of wrongs, and never comes to an end. Though it is read at weddings, Paul wrote it to a church divided over spiritual gifts, set between his teaching on the gifts (12) and on order in worship (14), to show “a way that is beyond comparison”. It ends: faith, hope and love last, “and of these three, the greatest is love.”

qa.question: What does 1 Corinthians teach about women in the church?
qa.answer: This is one of the places where Christians read Paul differently. In 11:2–16 he assumes that women pray and prophesy aloud in the gathering, and gives instructions about head coverings that some take as a lasting principle and others as guidance for the customs of that culture. In 14:34–35 he says the women are to keep silent in the churches; some read this as a limit on a particular disruptive kind of speaking, some as a wider rule of church order, and some think the verses were added to the letter later, since some manuscripts place them after verse 40. Paul also insists that “in the Lord there is no woman without man, and no man without woman” (11:11).

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.
